newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French troops patrol after Central African mutiny.
newsitem.headline: French troops patrol after Central African mutiny.

text.p: French troops patrolled the centre of the Central African Republic's capital Bangui on Saturday after army dissidents mutinied for a third time this year, military officers and witnesses said.
A French helicopter hovered over the city after the revolt, which according to army sources followed a bid to arrest an army captain related to former military leader Andre Kolingba.

President Ange-Felix Patasse, speaking in Rome where he is attending the World Food Summit, played down talk of a revolt. "It is not a mutiny. Some common law prisoners have escaped and are trying to create panic. That is all," he said.

But Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande, in a broadcast to the nation, urged all sides to hold fire and to return weapons to their armouries: "Nothing would be more serious for the country than a new bloody episode among its children."
Troops from former colonial power France, who put down a revolt that threatened to topple Patasse in May, patrolled the city centre with presidential guard loyalists.
"French soldiers have been deployed in Bangui to assure the safety of certain sensitive areas," a French official said in Paris.

France has an important military base in Central African Republic, one of the world's poorest countries, under a defence accord like it has with many former African colonies. Patasse, a civilian, invoked the accord in May to secure French help.
The base could play a key role in France's contribution to a multinational force to help refugees in Zaire.
Scattered firing could be heard early in the day but the city was calm by mid-afternoon when the curious started to venture out cautiously.

Markets remained closed throughout the city. There were no immediate reports of looting, such as accompanied the May mutiny and a pay revolt in April. Hospital sources say two people had been admitted with gunshot wounds.

Witnesses said dissidents had seized the general secretary of Patasse's ruling Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People (MLPC), Joseph Vermond Tchendo, and the head of the police national force, Ernest Latakpi.

The revolt began at Kassai Barracks about three km (two miles) from the city centre. "They broke into the armoury around midnight and stole arms and then firing broke out," a senior loyalist officer said.

Witnesses and military sources said the dissidents ventured out early on Saturday but later returned to Kassai barracks. A soldier contacted by telephone there said about 200 soldiers had gone to various areas to try to disarm militia loyal to Patasse.

Dissidents blamed the revolt on a bid on Friday to arrest a nephew of Kolingba, whom Patasse defeated in a 1993 presidential poll. In May, mutineers freed the nephew, Captain Annute Solet, who had been jailed on embezzlement and other charges.

Sources close to the dissidents said they had revived demands for wages from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering the Regiment for the Operational Defence of the Territory to Bouar, 80 km (50 miles) from Bangui. The regiment was heaviliy involved in the earlier revolts.

A national conference after the May revolt agreed on reforms to improve the lot of soldiers by creating a professional army with a fuller role in the life of the nation. But friction remains and Kolingba's Yakoma tribe is well-represented in the army.
